Why Your Chip Bag Has More Air Than Chips: Shrinkflation Explained

Inflation headlines say prices are 'cooling,' yet your grocery bill still feels heavier and snack packs look suspiciously lighter. Here is the psychology behind it.

By Juniper Brief Published 25 Nov 2026
Text size

1. You are not imagining it—the biscuit really did get smaller

Every shopper on Earth has had this exact moment: you pick up your favorite chocolate bar, detergent bottle, or bag of chips, squint at it, and think, 'Wait... didn't this used to be bigger?'

Yes. Yes it did. Economists call it shrinkflation—the art of keeping the price tag the same (or nudging it up slightly) while quietly trimming 10% to 15% of the product inside. Sometimes they even slap a cheerful 'NEW LOOK!' sticker on the front to distract you from the missing 40 grams.

2. Why companies shrink packages instead of just raising prices

Food and consumer brands know a weird quirk of human psychology: shoppers notice a $1 price jump immediately, but almost nobody reads the net weight in small print.

If a cookie pack jumps from ₹40 to ₹50 (or $4 to $5), half the aisle puts it back. If it stays at ₹40 while dropping from 100g to 85g, most people toss it into the cart without blinking. Multiply that 15-gram trim across 50 million packs, and the company protects its profit margin without triggering sticker shock.

3. 'Inflation is cooling' does NOT mean prices are going back down

Here is the single biggest confusion in everyday news: when governments say 'inflation fell from 7% to 3%', people hear 'things are getting cheaper!'

Sadly, no. Lower inflation just means prices are climbing slower—not walking backward. A 3% inflation rate on top of last year's 7% jump still means your basket is permanently ~10% pricier than two years ago. Actual falling prices (deflation) are super rare outside major recessions.

The 5-Second Supermarket Trick

Ignore the box size and look only at the price per 100g or per liter on the shelf tag. That tiny number exposes shrinkflation instantly.

4. The sneaky cousin: Skimpflation

When companies run out of ways to shrink the box, they switch to skimpflation: quietly swapping real cocoa butter for palm oil, thinning hotel housekeeping to every three days, or replacing human customer support with a cheerful chatbot that only knows three apologies. Knowing the trick doesn't stop it—but at least you won't feel crazy at the checkout counter.
